open_obligations: Note that Theorem 5.1 covers time-T, space-S oracle computations, while Irving et al.'s Theorem 1 covers all of PSPACE.

in.other_title: Theorem 5.1: (O(T log T), O(S log T), O(1))-debate protocol for time-T, space-S computations
in.rationale: Irving et al.'s Theorem 1 shows polynomial-step debate with a polynomial-time judge decides PSPACE under optimal play. Brown-Cohen et al.'s Theorem 5.1 gives a bisection protocol (A states a middle configuration, B picks a half) deciding any time-T, space-S oracle computation as an (O(T log T), O(S log T), O(1))-debate protocol, which the authors compare with doubly-efficient interactive proofs.
in.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: which computations a debate can decide, for PSPACE problems with a polynomial-time judge under optimal play versus time-T, space-S oracle Turing machine computations

in.other_title: Complexity analogy: reward modeling ~ NP, recursion depth k ~ k alternating quantifiers
in.rationale: Irving et al. show n-round debate with a polynomial-time judge corresponds to formulas with alternating quantifiers (Sigma_n P for fixed n, PSPACE with polynomially many rounds). Leike et al. credit this analogy to Irving et al. and argue reward modeling resembles NP while recursive reward modeling at depth k targets problems with k alternating quantifiers; no theorem is proved.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: the complexity-theory analogy between recursion depth in oversight schemes and alternating quantifiers

text: The authors show that an n-round debate judged by a polynomial-time algorithm H corresponds to formulas of the form 'exists x0 for all x1 ... H(q, x0, ...)', giving the class Sigma_n P for fixed n and PSPACE when the number of rounds grows polynomially in the question size. Theorem 1 states that for any problem L in PSPACE a polynomial-time judge can be chosen so that optimal play in a debate with polynomially many steps solves L.
title: Theorem 1: debate with a polynomial-time judge and optimal play decides PSPACE
